title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes Theorem 65 and gives three corollaries. Theorem 65: if p = 4n−1 is prime, no sum a²+b² with gcd(a,b)=1 is divisible by p. The proof uses §58. When p ≡ 3 (mod 4), −1 is a quadratic non-residue, which Euler derived earlier from primitive roots. So if b² ≡ 𝔟 (mod p) with 𝔟 ≠ 0, the class −𝔟 is never a square residue. Hence no square a² satisfies a²+b² ≡ 0 (mod p).

Corollary 1 (§66): a sum of two squares has no divisor of the form 4n−1 at all, prime or not. Any such divisor has a prime factor of that form. The stated exception is when both squares are divisible by the divisor.

Corollary 2 (§67): if a²+b² is divisible by a prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4), the quotient is not of the form 4n−1. It also has no prime factor of that form, unless a and b share such a factor. In that case the quotient contains the square of that factor.

Corollary 3 (§68) applies this to the quotients (a²+b²)/p in the tables on the previous pages, e.g. 2, 4, 9, 5, 2, 5, 10, 8, 13 for p = 37. Up to 32 the excluded numbers are 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, 14, 15, 19, 21, 22, 23, 24, 27, 28, 30, 31. The remaining ones are 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 25, 26, 29, 32. This is exactly the list of n ≤ 32 in which every prime q ≡ 3 (mod 4) occurs to an even power, i.e. the sums of two squares. Euler correctly keeps 9 and 18 (they contain 3²) and drops 27 (3³).

The purpose is to narrow down the possible quotients in the 'descent' approach to Fermat's two-squares theorem sketched on p. 116. If one could show that 1 always occurs among the quotients, then p itself would be a sum of two squares.
errors: Corollary 1's exception clause is imprecise for composite divisors. The correct exception is that both a and b are divisible by some prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) of the divisor, not by the divisor itself. Counterexample: 15 (of the form 4n−1) divides 3²+6² = 45, yet neither 9 nor 36 is divisible by 15. The intended statement for coprime squares is correct.

Corollary 3 only says which numbers are excluded. It does not prove that the remaining numbers actually occur as quotients, nor does it show that 1 occurs, which is what the proof needs. Euler is aware of this (see p. 116).

ideas.what: −1 is a quadratic non-residue modulo a prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4); hence such a prime divides no sum of two coprime squares
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier papers on sums of two squares, e.g. E228 'De numeris qui sunt aggregata duorum quadratorum' and E241; also E262

ideas.what: Prime factors ≡ 3 (mod 4) of a sum of two squares occur only through common factors of a and b, and then to even powers; the resulting list of admissible quotients up to 32
ideas.modern_name: Characterization of integers that are sums of two squares (necessity direction)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Fermat/Euler; full statement often credited to Euler, with Lagrange and Gauss giving systematic treatments
ideas.where_published: E228 and related papers on sums of two squares

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard corollaries of the non-residuosity of −1 modulo primes 4n−1, already known and proved by Euler elsewhere. The numerical lists are correct but routine. The only notable point is a small imprecision in Corollary 1.
